style_1_icd10.name: Complex regional pain syndrome I, unspecified
style_1_icd10.chapter: VI. Diseases of the nervous system / Neurology (G00-G99)

style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: AAN Practice Guidelines & EAN Guidelines on Neurological Disorders (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: ≥ 50% reduction in monthly attack/seizure frequency from baseline
Preservation of modified Rankin Scale score ≤ 2
Maintenance of baseline MoCA / MMSE cognitive scores

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Complex Regional Pain Syndrome focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Complex Regional Pain Syndrome require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Complex Regional Pain Syndrome.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.
Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.
Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.
Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Gabapentinoids, levetiracetam, and topiramate require strict renal dose adjustments.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Valproate, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are extensively metabolized by the liver; monitor serum levels.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Valproate is strictly contraindicated due to high neural tube and neurodevelopmental teratogenicity.
special_populations.elderly: Increased sensitivity to CNS sedatives, anticholinergics, and antiepileptic neurotoxicity; start low and titrate slowly.

style_3_monograph.summary: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a chronic pain condition. It causes intense pain, usually in the arms, hands, legs, or feet. It may happen after an injury, either to a nerve or to tissue in the affected area. Rest and time may only make it worse. Symptoms in the affected area are: Dramatic changes in skin temperature, color, or texture Intense burning pain Extreme skin sensitivity Swelling and stiffness in affected joints Decreased ability to move the affected body part The cause of CRPS is unknown. There is no specific diagnostic test. Your doctor will diagnose CRPS based on your signs and symptoms. There is no cure. It can get worse over time, and may spread to other parts of the body. Occasionally the symptoms go away, either temporarily or for good. Treatment focuses on relieving the pain, and can include medicines, physical therapy, and nerve blocks. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
style_3_monograph.treatment: There is no cure for CRPS, but the disease can be slowed. The main focus is on relieving the symptoms and helping people with this syndrome live as normal a life as possible. Physical and occupational therapy should be started as early as possible. Starting an exercise program and learning to keep joints and muscles moving may prevent the disease from getting worse. It can also help you do everyday activities. Medicines may be used, including pain medicines, corticosteroids, certain blood pressure medicines, bone loss medicines and antidepressants. Some type of talk therapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy or psychotherapy, can help teach the skills needed to live with long-term (chronic) pain. Surgical or invasive techniques that may be tried: Injected medicine that numbs the affected nerves or pain fibers around the spinal column (nerve block). Internal pain pump that directly delivers medicines to the spinal cord (intrathecal drug pump). Spinal cord stimulator, which involves placing electrodes (electrical leads) next to the spinal cord. A low-level electrical current is used to create a pleasant or tingling sensation in the painful area is the best way to reduce pain in some people. Surgery that cuts the nerves to destroy the pain (surgical sympathectomy), although it is unclear how many people this helps. It may also make symptoms worse in some people.
